title: Lob and Pip's Big Woods Rescue
markdown:
In the echoing ravines of Hazelhowe the wind sang its oldest songs through stoic stone, and the sun painted the hills in wide strokes, amber then amethyst, as if the day could not decide its clothes. Lob the young ogre lived in a cave smoothed by centuries of patient shuffling, a dwelling that smelled of river-cool and moonpetal. Often it held a secret sound: the delicate flutter of tiny wings. He was considerable, voice like distant thunder, hands that could shift a boulder and also cup a thimble. Guardian of Pip, a bat no larger than a thumb. Wings of midnight velvet. Chirps like the smallest silver bells. Who would have paired them? They had paired themselves. Afternoons: Lob tending pearly moonpetals that unfurled only for the moon’s gaze, Pip dancing with fireflies at the cave mouth, a happy blur against twilight. Peaceful. Familiar. A world with a rim.

He kept a whisper of unease for when the sun left the jagged peaks, a tremor no bigger than a dewdrop and somehow heavier than a boulder. The Whispering Woods pressed his home: a dense dark tangle, shadows that writhed into shapes his mind would not finish, rustling leaves like hushed disembodied talk. The fear was a heavy cloak, an ache in the ogre-heart. Every snapped twig a lurking beast, every gnarled branch a grasping claw, the sky itself a dark press. He rubbed a favourite river stone silky with years of anxious polish, an anchor when his thoughts spiralled. The woods were a well, and he stayed in the light, polishing until the stone knew his thumb-print by heart.

One sun-drenched afternoon, stone in hand, Pip zipped out with a joyful squeak. Lob’s broad face found a smile. The bat tumbled and darted, wings catching sun like slivers of emerald and ruby. Then a wind fiercer than any he knew roared the ravine, a lost-spirit howl, and with a cry like a falling icicle it snatched the speck and carried him to the looming edge. Gone. Breath hitch, sharp in the sudden quiet. Knees like saplings in a gale. The well had Pip in it. Night would bring the forest’s other tenants, owls with opinions, things that liked small warm meals. His stomach clenched. The stone was cool, a small vital fact. He could not wait. The trees seemed to murmur a warning; a prickle ran his back like needles. He filled his chest and went.

Sun softened to orange and rose, clouds in amber strokes. He clutched the stone and stepped past the first gnarled tree, bark like the wrinkled skin of a giant who had agreed to stand forever. Air cooler, light dimmer. The floor was a carpet of leaves, each clumsy boot-fall unnervingly loud, as if the woods were taking attendance. Owl-hoot. Twig-snap. Ferns like skeletal fingers on his tunic. Branches knitted a roof and cancelled the sky. In a wool-dark patch the drip of unseen water made his heart skip its job. Breath short, throat tight. For a long moment he would have turned, fear too great, too much like a blanket over the head. Eyes shut. Knuckles white on river-smooth. Pip, he whispered, a lifeline. The little face full of trust. He went on, because abandoning that face was a darker woods than this.

A faint squeak. High on a branch, silhouetted on a sliver of sky: Pip, weary, not swooping. Relief, then a new worry. The bat would not come to the big hand.

Lob needed someone who spoke woods. Flicker the elf lived near; he had avoided her out of shy awkwardness, hands too large, voice too much. He called, shaky. Tinkling laugh. A figure no taller than his knee, moss-stone eyes, summer-moonbeam hair.

“What brings you to this side?”

Warm neck. “I’ve lost Pip. I’m not good in the dark parts.” Shame, then the stone, his anchor. He held it out. “He won’t come down. A very good stone. If you help.”

She turned it, tracing cool. “Fine stone. You don’t need to give it. Coming here, and saying you were scared, is enough.” She looked up. “Pip. He missed you. He came even though he was frightened.”

A softer chirp, a hop, flutter onto the finger. Warm bundle in the palm.

“Thank you. I couldn’t have.”

“Next time the woods may be less of a monster. Visit to say hello, not only when something is lost.”

They walked the quicker way she knew, last sunlight dappling a path that had been there all along. A spring in steps that had been stones. Shadows still danced and were only shadows he had walked through. He noticed the delicate lace of a spider’s web catching last light like a string of tiny diamonds, and pine needles underfoot that smelled of comfort, not a warning. Still Lob of sunshine and open spaces. Also Lob who had gone in, spoken, and come out with a bat and an invitation to visit without an emergency.

The cave’s familiar warmth. Pip asleep on his chest, wings tucked neat. Lob set the river stone on its shelf, not as a shield against the dark, as a smooth fact that had been held enough for one day. Tomorrow the woods would still be woods. He might say hello.
characters: Lob (Lob the young ogre), Pip (mountain companions)
